catalog_quote: [Caron 2006, p.3] Zaar and Gùùs have three tone levels, the others only two. [fn.1] Hi is marked with an acute accent; Lo with a grave; Mid is left unmarked. ... In order to do so, we have picked one language from the Geji, Polci and Zeem clusters (resp. Bùù, Nyámzàk and Cààrí) and two from the Dass and Saya clusters ... [p.8] Cààrí (DANCHE) The survey of Cààrí was very short and the data collected is not very reliable. However, since Cààrí is the only surviving language of the Zeem subgroup, the other three (Zeem, Tule and Dokshi) being extinct, we have decided to include it here to give some idea of its TAM system. [Caron 2014, sect. 4.2] SBW languages as a rule have two imperative forms, depending on whether the addressee is singular or plural. The imperative is characterized by a specific tone pattern replacing the lexical tone pattern of the verb, and a suffix: -i for the singular, and –N for the plural: ... [4.2.2 Chaari (Zeem cluster)] In Chaari, the tone patterns of the Imperative are H for singular and LHL for plural. The plural suffix is -əne. [table: mbák, shoot -- mbákí -- mbàkə́nè; kám, take -- kámí -- kàmə́nè]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Chaari is treated as a register-tone language with two tone levels (H, L), like all South Bauchi West lects other than Zaar and Guus; tone is lexical on every morpheme and is morphologically active (imperative sg H vs pl LHL replacing the verb's lexical tones; sg/pl pronoun oppositions carried by tone). No source says anything about word stress or accent -- neither a stress rule nor a statement that stress is absent.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Caron (2003/2006) cautions that his first Chaari survey was very short and 'not very reliable'; the 2014 chapter rests on a later couple-of-weeks lexical/morphological survey.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statements concern lexical items and inflectional paradigms in citation/elicitation form; no word- vs phrase-level prosodic domain is discussed. The two-tone-levels remark is a group-level comparative statement in which Chaari is one of the explicitly sampled languages, not a dedicated phonological analysis of Chaari.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog dans1239 'Chaari' (historically labelled Danshe) = Cha'ari/Cààrí [cxh], created by ISO 639-3 CR 2022-030 from the old Zeem [zua] cluster. Caron's 'Cààrí (Danche)' data and the SIL 'Cha'ari' wordlist (collected in Danshe village, Toro LGA, Bauchi State) both refer to this variety. The sister lects Zeem [zem], Tulai [tvi], Dokshi/Lushi [dsk] and Dyarim [dyr, dyar1234] are distinct glottocodes; Dyarim (Blench 2005/2007, three phonetic tone levels, no stress statement) is already catalogued separately and its description must not be transferred to Chaari. The two-tone-levels statement quoted is a South-Bauchi-West group-level remark in which Chaari is one of the explicitly sampled languages.

sources.citation: Caron, Bernard (2011). Tonal Inversion in Geji and Pelu.
sources.note: The paper describes Geji and Pelu, two dialects of Geji proper (Northern sub-group of South Bauchi West), not Chaari. Chaari occurs only as a row in the Shimizu-1978 classification table on p.1 (Sub-group South > Zeem cluster > language Chaari, dialects Tule (extinct) and Chaari; Zeem (extinct), Dyarum (?)). No phonological data on Chaari at all. Even for Geji/Pelu the paper says nothing about stress or accent: it is a tone paper (footnote 2, p.2: 'Geji and Pelu are 3-tone language. tone.says: First-hand grammatical-tone data for Chaari (Zeem subgroup): imperative tone patterns H (singular) vs LHL (plural, with suffix -əne); elsewhere tone-marked Chaari lexical forms (H/L marking) and discussion of tonal plural marking in other SBW lects (Zakshi H vs L pronoun paradigms, floating tones in Langas/Guus). No tone inventory statement for Chaari or Zeem; nothing on Zeem proper.
